newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai army dismisses charges Karens forced back.
newsitem.headline: Thai army dismisses charges Karens forced back.

text.p: The Thai army on Friday dismissed charges by the United States and rights groups that ethnic Karen refugees arriving across the border from Burma were being forcibly repatriated.
But the general in charge of security in the affected border areas acknowledged that his forces had refused entry to some armed men trying to cross into Thailand with the refugees.
Thousands of Karen earlier this month fled fighting between Burmese troops and guerrillas of the Karen National Union (KNU), which is fighting for greater autonomy for eastern Karen state.
The U.S. State Department demanded that Thailand immediately stop the forcible repatriation, calling the border situation "very difficult and tragic".
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington was "deeply concerned" about the actions of the Thai army in forcibly repatriating some 900 Karen women.
London-based Amnesty International also accused the Thai military of forcibly repatriating the refugees.
But Major General Thaweep Suwannasing, commander of Thailand's 9th Army Division, denied this.

"There is no such forcible repatriation as they charge," he told Reuters by telephone. "The soldiers under my command have assisted hundreds of refugees, especially women, children and elderly people."
Thaweep's troops are responsible for security in the area between Thailand's Kanchanaburi province and Burma's eastern Tavoy district provinces.
"We allow in all the civilian refugees, but armed men believed to be guerrillas are banned from crossing the border," Thaweep said.
Karen refugee officials contacted at border camps, where some 70,000 refugees have been housed by Thailand since the early 1980s, supported the Thai army's claim.

"The Thai army did not push back any refugees. They relocated them from the jungle areas near the border to a safer location called Hauy Nam Long village," Htee Doe, a KNU official at one camp, told Reuters by telephone.
Some 1,515 Karen refugees who fled the latest Burmese offensive were now living in a safer camp deeper inside Thailand, he said.
"They were not pushed back. But about 300 young men who are believed to be KNU soldiers were not allowed to cross the border," Htee Doe said.
Burma has said it is willing to take back any Karen refugees wanting to return home.
The KNU, formed in 1948, has rejected several peace overtures from Burma's military government and remains one of the few ethnic guerrilla groups still fighting Rangoon.
Senior KNU sources said the group's moderate vice president, Swe Seing, wanted to hold peace talks with Rangoon but that hardline KNU leader General Bo Mya did not.
